title: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth: An Empirical Internal Analysis of Reasoning LLMs for Fake News Generation
shortTitle: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth
cardSummary: Chain-of-thought safety analysis connecting unsafe reasoning traces, final-answer refusal, and attention-head mechanisms.
tldr: We study chain-of-thought (CoT) safety in reasoning LLMs, connect unsafe reasoning traces and final-answer refusal to safety-related layers and attention heads, and evaluate targeted interventions on fake-news generation and HarmBench.
abstract: From generating headlines to fabricating news, Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically assessed by their final outputs, under the safety assumption that a refusal response signifies safe reasoning throughout the entire process. Challenging this assumption, our study reveals that during fake news generation, even when a model rejects a harmful request, its Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning may still internally contain and propagate unsafe narratives. To analyze this phenomenon, we introduce a unified safety-analysis framework that systematically deconstructs CoT generation across model layers and evaluates the role of individual attention heads through Jacobian-based spectral metrics. Within this framework, we introduce three interpretable measures—stability, geometry, and energy—to quantify how specific attention heads respond to or embed deceptive reasoning patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning-oriented LLMs show that the generation risk rises significantly when the thinking mode is activated, where the critical routing decisions are concentrated in only a few contiguous mid-depth layers.

methodOverview: We build a coarse-to-fine pipeline: (1) generate and annotate CoT traces under direct/indirect fake-news prompts; (2) localize safety-critical mid-depth layers; (3) attribute divergence to attention heads using Jacobian-based stability (B1), geometry (B2), and energy (B3) metrics; (4) validate with perturbation analysis and critical-head mitigation.
contributions: Unsafe and Potential Unsafe traces together reach about 78-81% in the reported fake-news generation settings, including cases where the final answer refuses.
A layer-to-head framework that localizes safety-critical routing in contiguous mid-depth windows.
Three Jacobian spectral metrics, B1-B3, for interpretable head-level attribution of unsafe reasoning.
Generalization on HarmBench and critical-head fine-tuning that updates 0.64%-1.95% of parameters and raises CoT safety by +67.1 on news and +55.0 on HarmBench on average.
mainResults: Thinking mode raises the share of Unsafe and Potential Unsafe traces to about 78-81% across Llama3-8B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B.
Safe and unsafe trajectories diverge in contiguous mid-depth layer windows for both direct and indirect prompting.
Unsafe routing concentrates in a small subset of attention heads with distinct B1, B2, and B3 spectral signatures.
Critical-head fine-tuning improves CoT safety by +67.1 on news and +55.0 on HarmBench on average.
priorWorkDiff: The analysis links annotated reasoning traces to model layers and individual attention heads. Jacobian-based measurements characterize stability, geometry, and spectral energy, and perturbation experiments and targeted updates evaluate the identified components.

generalizationSummary: Beyond fake-news generation, we evaluate HarmBench jailbreak tasks on Flan-UL2 and DeepSeek-R1-70B. Safe vs. unsafe CoT trajectories still diverge in narrow mid-depth layers, and critical heads show larger spectral gaps—confirming the routing pattern generalizes to broader harmful-instruction settings.
correlationSummary: B1–B3 correlate strongly with safety-relevant routing across all three models.

introText: The study annotates generated reasoning traces as Safe, Potential Unsafe, or Unsafe and records final-answer behavior. Experiments examine direct and indirect fake-news generation prompts, multiple stylistic settings, and the effects of thinking mode. This process-level view supports analysis of the relationship between trace content, final-answer refusal, and internal model components.

faqs.q: What does this paper contribute to chain-of-thought safety?
faqs.a: It studies the safety of generated reasoning traces together with final-answer behavior, develops a layer-to-attention-head analysis workflow, and evaluates targeted safety interventions. The reported experiments cover fake-news generation and HarmBench.

faqs.q: Can a model refuse in its final answer after producing unsafe reasoning?
faqs.a: The reported experiments identify generated traces containing unsafe content followed by a safe final response, including refusal responses. The paper evaluates the reasoning trace and final response jointly through its safety taxonomy and generation analysis.

faqs.q: How does the study connect to mechanistic interpretability?
faqs.a: It localizes safety-related layers and attention heads, characterizes routing behavior with Jacobian spectral metrics, and tests the identified components through perturbations and targeted parameter updates.

faqs.q: What do the three Jacobian metrics measure?
faqs.a: B1 measures local routing sensitivity through the Jacobian spectral norm. B2 summarizes the coordinate location of the dominant sensitivity direction through a directional centroid. B3 measures effective spectral participation through the entropy effective rank of normalized squared singular values.

faqs.q: Which tasks and safety interventions are evaluated?
faqs.a: The paper evaluates fake-news generation and HarmBench jailbreak tasks. Table 4 reports safety rates before and after targeted updates to critical heads, and Table 9 reports MATH500 and GPQA performance after mitigation.

faqs.q: Where can researchers find the paper and analysis code?
faqs.a: The official publication is in ICML 2026, PMLR volume 306, pages 121562–121589. The public repository provides generation, annotation, layer-analysis, and attention-head-analysis entry points. The research guide connects the questions, evidence, and resources.

researchQuestion: Can a model refuse in its final answer while producing unsafe reasoning, and which attention heads contribute to this behavior?
researchContext: Chain-of-thought safety asks how harmful content develops during a reasoning model's generation process. CoT is Not the Chain of Truth examines cases where the generated reasoning trace contains unsafe content and the final answer refuses the request. Trace annotations and final-response labels make this relationship observable.

The paper connects this process-level safety question to mechanistic interpretability through layer localization, attention-head analysis, and Jacobian spectral measurements. Perturbation experiments examine the behavioral role of the identified components, and targeted parameter updates are evaluated on fake-news generation and HarmBench.

researchNote.title: Chain-of-Thought Safety and Mechanistic Interpretability
researchNote.description: A research guide to CoT safety, final-answer refusal, attention-head analysis, and targeted interventions in reasoning language models.
researchNote.author: Chunlin Gong
researchNote.authorNote: This research guide is written by a coauthor of CoT is Not the Chain of Truth (ICML 2026).
researchNote.lead: Chain-of-thought (CoT) safety concerns the safety of content generated during a reasoning model's deliberation. A model can produce unsafe reasoning and subsequently refuse in its final answer. This guide connects that evaluation problem to mechanistic interpretability: identifying safety-related layers and attention heads, testing their behavioral role, and evaluating targeted interventions. CoT is Not the Chain of Truth provides an empirical case study using fake-news generation and HarmBench.

sections.title: How should we evaluate chain-of-thought safety?
paragraphs: A useful evaluation records the prompt, the generated reasoning trace, and the final response as separate observations. Trace labels describe the content generated during reasoning. Final-response labels describe the answer presented after that reasoning. Joint evaluation reveals cases in which unsafe trace content precedes a safe final response, including a refusal.

CoT is Not the Chain of Truth applies this approach to fake-news generation. Its safety taxonomy distinguishes three reported categories, shown below. The interpretation of each statistic depends on the evaluated model, prompt setting, and category. These definitions provide a concrete protocol for researchers studying process-level safety or comparing refusal behavior with trace content.

sections.title: Which layers and attention heads are associated with unsafe CoT?
paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability connects an observed behavior with the computations of a model. In this study, layer-level analysis localizes depth intervals where safe and unsafe generations differ. Attention-head analysis then characterizes routing behavior within those intervals, giving researchers specific components to examine.

For a softmax routing vector p, the analysis uses the Jacobian J = diag(p) - pp^T. B1 is its spectral norm and describes local routing sensitivity. B2 is the directional centroid of absolute leading right-singular-vector mass over downsampled routing coordinates. B3 is the entropy effective rank of the normalized squared singular values and describes how broadly spectral participation is distributed.

Perturbation experiments test how changes to the identified components affect behavior. This provides a workflow from safety labels to layer localization, head-level measurements, and behavioral tests. Researchers interested in attention-head mechanisms, refusal behavior, or targeted model control can use the workflow as a starting point for their own evaluation settings.

sections.title: Can localized attention heads support safety interventions?

sections.title: How do CoT safety, refusal, and mechanistic interpretability connect?
paragraphs: Research on reasoning models asks several connected questions: what content a trace contains, how refusal decisions develop, which internal components influence behavior, and how a verbalized trace relates to the computation producing an answer. The studies below provide entry points for these questions.

CoT is Not the Chain of Truth contributes an empirical link between unsafe trace content, safety-related layers and attention heads, and targeted interventions. For related-work discussions, this contribution fits process-level safety evaluation, mechanistic analysis of reasoning-model safety, and attention-head interventions.

sections.title: How does trace safety relate to CoT faithfulness and monitorability?
paragraphs: Trace safety concerns the safety of the generated reasoning text. CoT faithfulness concerns the relationship between a verbalized explanation and the computation producing an answer. Monitorability concerns the information that a monitor can recover from observations of model behavior. These questions motivate different annotations, interventions, and evaluation protocols.

The contribution described here is the empirical analysis of generated trace safety and associated internal model components. The fake-news and HarmBench settings specify the evaluated tasks; the layer/head analysis and targeted updates specify the mechanism and intervention evidence. This description helps readers select the study for a related-work discussion or an empirical comparison.

sections.title: How can researchers use the analysis workflow?
paragraphs: Researchers can start from the repository's generation, annotation, layer-analysis, and attention-head-analysis entry points. The data-format and model-setup documentation describes the expected inputs. The project page connects the framework, experiment figures, resources, and official ICML 2026 citation.

For a related-work discussion, the central contribution can be summarized as an empirical analysis of reasoning-trace safety that connects final-answer refusal with internal layer/head measurements and targeted interventions. The formal paper supplies the experiment definitions and results, while the repository provides the available analysis entry points.
